questions.q: Given `double price = 182.35; double* ptr = &price;`, what does `*ptr = 190.00;` do?
options: Creates a new double called ptr with value 190.00
Changes price itself to 190.00, since ptr holds price's address
Causes a compile error because ptr is a pointer
Only changes a local copy, leaving price unchanged
questions.explain: Dereferencing ptr with * accesses the memory ptr points to, which is price's own storage. Assigning through it changes price itself — no copy is involved.

questions.q: Why should code check `if (ptr != nullptr)` before dereferencing a pointer that might be null?
options: It isn't necessary; dereferencing a null pointer is always safe in C++
Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behavior, so checking first avoids crashes or unpredictable results
nullptr automatically converts to 0.0 when dereferenced
The check is only needed for pointers to int, not double
questions.explain: Dereferencing nullptr is undefined behavior in C++ — commonly a crash, but not guaranteed. Guarding with a null check before dereferencing is standard defensive practice.

questions.q: Given `double prices[3] = {100.1, 100.2, 100.3}; double* p = prices;`, what does `*(p + 1)` evaluate to?
options: 100.1, because pointer arithmetic always returns the first element
A memory address, not a value
100.2, because pointer arithmetic advances by sizeof(double), landing on the second element
A compile error
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic advances by the size of the pointed-to type. p + 1 moves one double's worth of bytes forward, landing on prices[1], which is 100.2.

questions.q: What does `const double* p1` mean, as opposed to `double* const p2`?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
p1 is a pointer to a const double (can repoint p1, can't modify *p1); p2 is a const pointer to a double (can modify *p2, can't repoint p2)
p1 cannot be dereferenced at all; p2 can
p1 is always faster than p2
questions.explain: Reading from the asterisk: const double* p1 is a pointer to const data — the pointed-to value can't change, but p1 can be repointed. double* const p2 is a const pointer — p2 itself can't be reassigned, but the value it points to can be modified.

questions.q: According to the decision rule in this lesson, when should you reach for a raw pointer parameter instead of a reference?
options: Whenever the type is larger than 8 bytes
When the argument might legitimately be absent — nullptr represents a real, meaningful state
Whenever performance matters at all
Never — pointers should always be avoided in modern C++
questions.explain: References can never be null, so they can't represent 'no object.' A pointer (or, better, a smart pointer) is the right tool specifically when the argument might legitimately not exist.
